title: GenAI generates GenAI – A Diffusion Model That Generates Neural Networks
content:
⚠️ WORK IN PROGRESS — EXPERIMENTAL RESEARCH. This project is an
exploration, not a conclusion. We are studying whether a diffusion model
can generate neural networks instead of images; results so far are
provisional, the corpus and model are small, quality varies, and everything
here may change as the investigation continues. Nothing in this repository
is final or production-ready.
NNGen is a generator of generative models: a diffusion model with a text-to-image architecture that, instead of generating images, generates a GenAI model — a working neural network whose weights it denoises from pure noise, guided by a text description.
Where text-to-image systems learn the mapping caption → pixels, NNGen learns caption → network weights: describe a behavior in English, and the model produces a brand-new neural network that performs it. Same machinery — UNet, v-prediction, cosine schedule, DDIM sampling, classifier-free guidance — one level of abstraction higher: from pictures of things, to the things themselves.
Prompt:  "A tiny MLP drawing agent: it drives a pen on a 2D canvas
          to trace a five-pointed star."
             │  diffusion sampling (DDIM, CFG)
             ▼
Output:  a NEW neural network (~1.6k parameters) that draws a star,
         exported as safetensors + rollout GIF + quality metrics
Training pairs mirror the text-to-image recipe — (image, caption) becomes (network, caption):
- The "image" is a 6×32×32 weight canvas: the six parameter tensors of a
fixed-size controller MLP (8 → 32 → 32 → 8, ~1.6k parameters), laid out
like image channels with a validity mask, z-normalized into [-1, 1] — the
same regime as pixels.
- The caption is an English description of the behavior ("a tiny MLP that drives a pen to trace a five-pointed star"), encoded by a frozen MiniLM and injected via cross-attention.
- The corpus is self-generated: thousands of controllers are trained through differentiable mini-environments for games and animation tasks (behavior cloning from analytic experts where needed), filtered by strict held-out rollout criteria, and captioned from templates. No human-labeled data — the dataset is manufactured by compute.
A compact text-conditioned UNet (2.3M parameters, mvp preset) learns to
denoise weight canvases. Sampling from a prompt yields a network that is
decoded and executed directly in its environment.
The drawing demo includes circle, square, triangle, pentagon, star, star6, spiral, line and arc — while hexagon and octagon are deliberately held out of the corpus to measure compositional generalization: if the model draws a hexagon it has never seen, it learned the concept of a regular polygon, not a lookup table of shapes.
python webapp/server.py --port 17656     # then open http://localhost:17656
A standard-library-only Python server (no framework, no build step) with all
URLs relative, ready to host behind a reverse proxy at any domain/sub-path.
It serves the English documentation, a live demo (prompt → generated network →
rollout GIF + weight heatmap + metrics via a background job queue) and a small
JSON API (POST api/generate, GET api/job/<id>, GET api/status).
## Pretrained generator & dataset (included)
The repository ships with everything needed to run and reproduce the drawing
experiment without re-training from scratch:
| file | what it is | size |
|---|---|---|
| `weights/nngen_draw_mvp.safetensors` | the trained diffusion generator (EMA UNet weights, 2.3M params, v-prediction) | ~9 MB |
| `data/corpus_draw/weights.safetensors` | the full training corpus: 2,916 controller networks (raw flat weights) | ~19 MB |
| `data/corpus_draw/meta.jsonl` | one record per network: task, English caption, rollout score, success, split | ~1 MB |
| `data/corpus_draw/stats.json` | per-tensor normalization statistics used by the weight canvas | <1 KB |
The cached MiniLM token embeddings are not included (~143 MB); regenerate them
deterministically from the captions with the command below. Full training
checkpoints (model + optimizer + EMA) are also not included — the slim release
file is what inference needs.
With a fresh clone, this works out of the box:
```bash
python -m dnn.generate \
  --prompt "A tiny MLP drawing agent: it drives a pen on a 2D canvas to trace a closed regular hexagon." \
  --task draw_hexagon            # checkpoint auto-resolves to the release weightspip install -r requirements.txt
# 1. mass-train controllers through the differentiable environments
#    (~2-3 h on 8 CPU cores; deterministic seeds per task/batch)
python -m dnn.corpus.train_controllers --tasks draw_circle,draw_square,draw_triangle,draw_pentagon,draw_star,draw_star6,draw_spiral,draw_line,draw_arc \
    --per-task 300 --out data/corpus_draw
# 2. cache text embeddings (one-time MiniLM download, ~1 min)
python -m dnn.corpus.embed_captions --corpus data/corpus_draw
# 3. train the generator (mvp preset = CPU-feasible: ~3.5 h on 8 cores, 1500 steps)
python -m dnn.train_diffusion --config mvp --corpus data/corpus_draw --run runs/draw_mvp
# 4. generate a network from a prompt (CLI) — writes net + GIF + report
python -m dnn.generate --prompt "..." --task draw_hexagon --ckpt runs/draw_mvp/ckpt.pt --out runs/demo
# 5. quantitative eval: generated vs teacher vs random on validation captions
python -m dnn.eval --ckpt runs/draw_mvp/ckpt.pt
# 6. the website
python webapp/server.py --port 17656
# export a slim release checkpoint like the one shipped in weights/
python scripts/export_release.py --ckpt runs/draw_mvp/ckpt.pt --out weights/nngen_draw_mvp.safetensors
Step 1 keeps only networks that trace their whole curve on a held-out episode (point accuracy, full-curve coverage, closure and pace); failed candidates are discarded and the trainer's retry budget absorbs the pass-rate. Step 3's validation loss and step 5's benchmark are the objective measures of progress.
dnn/
  config.py            fixed sizes + presets (smoke/mvp/small/base)
  controller.py        canonical MLP, weight canvas, normalization, stats
  text_encoder.py      frozen MiniLM wrapper
  tasks/               mini-environments + draw shapes, registry
  corpus/              caption templates, batch trainer (expert cloning),
                       incremental storage, embedding cache
  diffusion/           cosine schedule, UNet (cross-attn), DDIM + CFG, EMA
  train_diffusion.py   training loop (EMA, checkpoints, resume, val loss)
  generate.py          prompt → network → rollout → artifacts
  eval.py              generated vs teacher vs random benchmark
  render.py            behavior GIFs and weight heatmaps
webapp/
  server.py            NNGen website + demo API (stdlib HTTP, port 17656)
  pages/, static/      English documentation and demo UI
tests/                 canvas round-trip, tasks, diffusion, e2e pipeline
scripts/               demos and utilities
- This is an ongoing exploration. The core question — can diffusion generate neural networks usefully? — is still open, and we are still studying it: expect changes, small numbers, and dead ends published as honestly as successes.
- Research prototype: one fixed-size controller architecture, simple
behaviors, CPU-only training (the mvp preset trains in a few hours on 8
cores; a GPU multiplies corpus size and model capacity by an order of
magnitude).
- The generator can only produce behaviors resembling its training corpus — and, in the best case, interpolate between them (that is exactly what the held-out hexagon/octagon experiment measures).
- Success is measured, not promised: eval.py reports generated networks
against their corpus teachers and random initialization on unseen captions.
This project sits in the emerging field the survey "A Survey of Weight Space Learning: Understanding, Representation, and Generation" (arXiv:2603.10090) calls Weight Space Generation. Section 4.2.1 — Conditional Weight Generation describes exactly the family of approaches NNGen belongs to: synthesizing model parameters specialized for a task or semantic c

report.summary: An experimental open-source project uses a text-to-image-style diffusion model to generate the weights of tiny working neural networks — not images — from English prompts.
report.background: Training a neural network normally means running an optimization loop. Weight-space learning asks a different question: can a model learn the distribution of trained weights themselves and simply sample new ones? The idea has ancestors in hypernetworks, learned optimizers and model merging, and it mirrors diffusion's spread into proteins, molecules and code — generative models of artifacts rather than pictures. NNGen sits in what a recent survey (arXiv:2603.10090, section 4.2.1, conditional weight generation) calls Weight Space Generation. The practical appeal is obvious: if sampling weights were as cheap as sampling pixels, some of the compute spent on training could be traded for inference. The obstacle is that weights are not pixels — they are permutation-symmetric, architecture-bound and hard to score. NNGen is a deliberately small, CPU-feasible probe of whether the recipe transfers at all.
key_points: Weights are reformatted as images. The six parameter tensors of a fixed 8→32→32→8 controller MLP (~1.6k parameters) are laid out as a 6×32×32 canvas with a validity mask, z-normalized per tensor into [-1, 1]. Once weights look like pixels, ordinary text-to-image machinery applies unchanged: UNet with cross-attention, v-prediction, cosine noise schedule, DDIM sampling, classifier-free guidance.

The dataset is manufactured, not labeled. Thousands of controllers are trained through differentiable mini-environments for drawing and animation tasks, using behavior cloning from analytic experts, then filtered by strict held-out rollout criteria (curve coverage, closure, pace). Survivors are captioned from templates; the shipped corpus holds 2,916 networks and about 1 MB of metadata. No human annotation is involved.

Generalization is tested with held-out shapes. Circle, square, triangle, pentagon, star, spiral, line and arc are in the corpus; hexagon and octagon are deliberately excluded. If the model draws a hexagon it has never seen, the authors argue, it captured the concept of a regular polygon rather than memorizing a lookup table. That is the experiment's real scientific payload.

The claims are scoped small and stated honestly. The generator is a 2.3M-parameter UNet, the outputs are 1.6k-parameter MLPs, and the whole thing trains in roughly 3.5 hours on 8 CPU cores. The repository is labeled work in progress with provisional results, quality that varies, and a warning that it can only reproduce or interpolate behaviors resembling its training corpus.

Everything ships reproducibly. A 9 MB safetensors checkpoint, a 19 MB weight corpus, normalization stats, a CLI generate command, a quantitative eval script comparing generated networks against their teachers and random initialization, plus a standard-library web demo with a JSON API.
report.impact: For the AI industry, NNGen is a pointer rather than a product: it shows that conditional weight generation can be wired up end to end with off-the-shelf diffusion components and a self-generated corpus, and it names the real bottleneck — evaluating weights requires executing them, which is far messier than scoring an image. Expect more work on weight-space benchmarks and on scaling beyond fixed-size architectures. For developers, the immediately useful parts are the pipeline pattern (synthetic corpus, rollout-based filtering, prompt-to-artifact serving) and the honest release hygiene. For regular users, nothing changes yet: this cannot generate a general-purpose model from a sentence, only tiny specialist controllers whose behavior lives inside a toy environment.
report.tools: Start with the NNGen repository itself (github.com/vagrillo/nngen) — the pretrained drawing checkpoint and corpus are included, so you can run a prompt-to-network demo in minutes. Read the framing survey, A Survey of Weight Space Learning (arXiv:2603.10090), especially section 4.2.1. Compare with Neural Network Diffusion and the hypernetwork literature. On the practical side, Hugging Face safetensors for weight handling, sentence-transformers MiniLM for frozen text conditioning, and the diffusers library for UNet, DDIM and classifier-free guidance building blocks.
